new_statements.quote: Lexical stress in Maybrat seems to be weakly phonemic, as it cannot be fully predicted. However, some generalisations which predict stress can be made: stress can only fall on a phonemic, non-reduced V. As a rule, main stress, marked ‘ ˈ ’, falls on the initial syllable of bisyllabic words, as illustrated in (40), and most trisyllabic words, as illustrated in (41). In trisyllabic words, a secondary stress, marked ‘ˌ’, may be heard on the final syllable. [...] The epenthetic vowel [ə] cannot receive stress, so it is ‘skipped’ in stress assignment

new_statements.locator: sec. 2.4.1 'Lexical stress', p. 38 (dialect list incl. Karon: sec. 1.7, p. 9; Karon forms with stress marks p. 11)

However, some generalisations which predict stress can be made: stress can only fall on a phonemic, non-reduced V. As a rule, main stress, marked.., falls on the initial syllable of bisyllabic words, as illustrated in (40), and most trisyllabic words, as illustrated in (41). In trisyllabic words, a secondary stress, marked.., may be heard on the final syllable.' then examples (40)-(41), then 'The epenthetic vowel [schwa] cannot receive stress, so it is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Maybrat as described from the Mayhapeh (Ayawasi) dialect: main stress on the first syllable containing a full (non-schwa) vowel in two- and most three-syllable words; epenthetic schwa is invisible to stress; forms of the shape Cə-Ci-jV take final stress; po- nominalisations stress the first full syllable of the stem; compounds take main stress on the second member. Dol classifies Karon (= Karon Dori, Senopi/Fef) as a Maybrat dialect and her Karon citations ([ˈgijAm], [məˈdAx], [ˈtijain]) are stress-marked consistently with this rule, but she gives no stress statement specific to Karon.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In trisyllables a secondary stress may be heard on the final syllable; in words of more than three syllables (compounds) secondary stress falls on alternating syllables to the left and right of the main stress, with clash avoidance.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-position doublets (ˈkapan ~ kaˈpan 'eel', ˈumam ~ uˈmam 'sweat', etc.) and unpredictable non-initial forms (paˈyir 'rainbow', faˈyir 'decorate', oˈra 'garden', aˈfi 'roof', aˈyo 'sun'); Dol calls stress 'weakly phonemic'. Footnote 20 (p. 27): Brown 1991 found stress fully phonemic in the Ayamaru (Maymaru) dialect with different placements ([aˈmax] vs Ayawasi [ˈamAx] 'house'), so stress placement is known to vary between Maybrat dialects — extrapolation to Karon Dori is not safe.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress in citation forms (sec. 2.4.1); sec. 2.4.2 treats connected speech separately (alternating rhythm, clash resolution by schwa epenthesis or destressing). IDENTITY CAVEAT: the description is of the Mayhapeh dialect of Maybrat (maib1239), which is already in the catalog from Dol 1999 via StressTyp2; it covers karo1303 only through Dol's classification of Karon as a Maybrat dialect, not through Karon data.
new_statements.identity_note: No source opened describes Karon Dori (karo1303; self-name Miyah/Miyakh, also Maiyach, Karon Gunung; Senopi-Fef area, Tambrauw) from its own data. The quoted statement is Dol 2007's rule for the Mayhapeh (Ayawasi) dialect of Maybrat = Glottolog maib1239 'Mai Brat', which is already in the catalog (unit 'Mai Brat', Dol 1999:42 via StressTyp2). Dol (sec. 1.7) classifies Karon (Dori) as one of six Maybrat dialects (72% lexical cognacy with Mayhapeh; earlier surveys Voorhoeve 1987b and Berry & Berry 1987 listed it as a separate language, as Glottolog does). Brown 1991 (Maymaru/Ayamaru dialect, also maib1239) reports phonemic free stress, so stress placement differs even among Maybrat dialects; entering Dol's initial-stress rule under karo1303 would both duplicate maib1239 and over-extend the data. Syufi et al. 2023 note that 'Karon Dori' formerly covered two varieties, Miyah and Irires; Pratiwi 2010 (Irires) and Wodi 2011 (Miyakh) are the variety-specific phonologies.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4.1 p.38 (Mayhapeh/Ayawasi dialect): lexical stress 'weakly phonemic'; as a rule main stress on the initial syllable of bi- and most trisyllabic words, schwa skipped, secondary stress may be heard on final syllable of trisyllables; compounds stress the 2nd member; doublets and a few unpredictable forms (pa'yir, o'ra, a'fi). Sec. 1.7 pp.9-11 lists Karon (Senopi, Fef) = Karon Dori as one of six Maybrat dialects (72% cognate with Mayhapeh) and cites Karon forms with stress marks ([ˈgijAm] 'they are ill', [məˈdAx] 'dog', [ˈtijain]) but makes no Karon-specific stress statement. Footnote 20…
